blocks.text: 1. Adam
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933456-140925306.png

The Adam preview already given at the close of the RMSProp topic set up exactly what this topic now covers in full. Adam directly combines RMSProp's per-weight adaptive rate with Momentum's own accumulated velocity, both already covered fully in their own dedicated topics.

It is arguably the single most widely used optimizer across all of modern Deep Learning practice today, worth understanding in genuine, complete depth given how commonly it actually gets reached for in real, practical training.
2. Two Moments, Tracked Together
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933456-647612041.png

Adam tracks two genuinely separate running quantities, called moments. The first moment is a running average of the gradients themselves, directly echoing Momentum's own accumulated velocity, already covered in its own dedicated topic.

The second moment is a running average of the squared gradients, directly echoing RMSProp's own running average, also already covered in its own dedicated topic, meaning Adam genuinely tracks both ideas simultaneously, rather than choosing just one.

blocks.text: 3. The Combined Update
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933457-943504624.png

Adam divides the first moment, the momentum-style direction already covered in the previous section, by the square root of the second moment, the RMSProp-style adaptive scale also already covered in that same section.

This produces one single, combined update that genuinely benefits from both ideas at once: a smoothed, momentum-informed direction, scaled individually per weight based on that weight's own recent gradient magnitude history.
4. Bias Correction
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933457-885686721.png

A genuine, subtle detail worth understanding is that both moving averages start at exactly zero, before any real updates have actually happened yet. This biases early estimates artificially toward zero, since there has not been enough accumulated history yet for the running averages to genuinely reflect the actual gradient statistics.

Adam applies a specific bias correction to counteract this, especially important during early training, directly counteracting this genuine, real startup effect so the very first several updates are not artificially, misleadingly small.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Skipping bias correction, an easy mistake in a hand-rolled implementation, can cause noticeably poor behavior during the first several training steps, even though the optimizer eventually settles into normal, expected behavior once the moving averages accumulate enough real history.

blocks.text: 5. Adam's Common Hyperparameters

This connects back to hyperparameters, a concept already established throughout this course. Beta1, controlling the first moment, has a common, standard default of 0.9, directly echoing Momentum's own coefficient, already covered in its own dedicated topic.

Beta2, controlling the second moment, has a common, standard default of 0.999, directly echoing RMSProp's own decay parameter, also already covered in its own topic, meaning Adam's default hyperparameters are themselves genuinely inherited from the two ideas it actually combines.
6. A Genuine, Real Practical Advantage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933457-804363831.png

A genuine, real practical fact is that Adam often works well right out of the box, with minimal manual tuning needed beyond its own standard, common default hyperparameter values already covered in the previous section.

This is a genuinely significant reason for its extremely widespread, default adoption across modern practice, since a practitioner can often simply reach for Adam with its standard defaults and get genuinely reasonable results, without needing extensive, careful hyperparameter tuning first.
7. Genuine, Real Criticisms
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933457-583046285.png

This connects back to the empirical tradeoffs already covered throughout this module. Adam does not always generalize quite as well as plain, well-tuned Stochastic Gradient Descent, already shared with the traditional Machine Learning course, on certain specific problems.

This is a genuine, ongoing area of research and real debate within the field, worth knowing about even though Adam remains, overall, an extremely common and generally reliable, sensible default choice for most practical training scenarios.
8. A Preview of AdamW
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444933458-602298827.png

This connects forward to AdamW, the very next topic in this module. AdamW fixes a genuine, specific technical issue with how Adam interacts with weight decay, covered in further practical depth in the Regularization Techniques module later in this course.

Understanding Adam clearly first, covered fully throughout this topic, sets up direct, considerable groundwork for understanding exactly what AdamW actually changes, and why that specific change genuinely matters in practice.
9. Why Adam Is Genuinely the Common Starting Point

Adam works well across a genuinely wide range of problems, with minimal manual tuning needed, already covered throughout this topic, making it the practical, default choice for most new Deep Learning projects starting out.

This is not a claim that Adam is always the theoretically optimal choice, exactly the genuine criticism already covered earlier in this topic, but it is a genuinely reasonable, well-justified starting point before considering more specialized alternatives for a specific, particular problem.
10. Worked Example
The example below implements Adam from scratch, directly demonstrating its two moments and bias correction covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np

def adam_update(weight, gradient, m, v, t, learning_rate=0.001, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, epsilon=1e-8):
    m = beta1 * m + (1 - beta1) * gradient              # first moment: momentum-style
    v = beta2 * v + (1 - beta2) * gradient ** 2          # second moment: RMSProp-style

    m_corrected = m / (1 - beta1 ** t)                    # bias correction
    v_corrected = v / (1 - beta2 ** t)

    weight -= learning_rate * m_corrected / (np.sqrt(v_corrected) + epsilon)
    return weight, m, v

weight = 1.0
m, v = 0.0, 0.0

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
gradients = rng.normal(loc=0.3, scale=0.05, size=50)

for t, gradient in enumerate(gradients, start=1):
    weight, m, v = adam_update(weight, gradient, m, v, t)

print(f"Final weight after 50 Adam updates: {weight:.4f}")
print(f"Final first moment (momentum-style): {m:.4f}")
print(f"Final second moment (RMSProp-style): {v:.4f}")
print("\nBoth moments were tracked and combined together, exactly the combined update covered in this topic")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example implements bias correction explicitly, dividing each moment by 1 minus its own decay rate raised to the current step count, exactly the mechanism covered earlier in this topic that keeps early updates from being artificially small.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Adam directly combines RMSProp's per-weight adaptive rate with Momentum's own accumulated velocity.
It tracks two moments: a running average of gradients, and a running average of squared gradients.
It divides the momentum-style first moment by the square root of the RMSProp-style second moment.
Bias correction counteracts both moving averages starting at zero, important especially during early training.
Its common defaults, beta1 at 0.9 and beta2 at 0.999, are directly inherited from Momentum and RMSProp.
It often works well right out of the box, a significant reason for its extremely widespread adoption.
It does not always generalize quite as well as well-tuned plain SGD, a genuine, ongoing area of research.
AdamW, covered next, fixes a specific technical issue with how Adam interacts with weight decay.
Next up: AdamW, a targeted refinement addressing exactly this specific, real technical issue.
